 1 I.       INTRODUCTION

 2          This motion to certify a class is straightforward—just like the ones in Frasco, Prudential

 3 Financial, and Rodriguez, where the courts certified classes of consumers tracked by identical or

 4 similar tracking technologies. Frasco v. Flo Health, Inc., 349 F.R.D. 557 (N.D. Cal. 2025) (certifying

 5 class based on the same liability expert here, Dr. Egelman, who Capital One doesn’t challenge);

 6 Torres v. Prudential Fin., Inc., 2024 WL 4894289, at *8 (N.D. Cal. Nov. 26, 2024); Rodriguez v.

 7 Google LLC, 2024 WL 38302, at *9 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 3, 2024). Capital One ran a single, standardized

 8 scheme on its credit card application webpages—deploying the same tracking and server-to-server

 9 technologies, under the same inadequate form disclosures, collecting and transmitting applicants’

10 information in the same way. It compensated no one for use of their personal and financial

11 information, though Capital One valued that data—                                               . That

12 common course of conduct is the whole ballgame. The core questions—what tools Capital One

13 deployed, what they collected and transmitted as reflected by Capital One’s records, what Capital

14 One told (or didn’t tell) users in form disclosures, the lack of compensation for use of personal and

15 financial information, and whether that conduct was lawful—are common and predominant issues

16 that rise or fall on common proof from Capital One’s records and common legal theories.

17          Capital One’s opposition never gets around that problem. Instead, it tries to muddy the waters

18 by dressing up common merits questions as individualized. But Rule 23 is not defeated by smoke and

19 mirrors. The question is whether individual issues overwhelm the common ones. Here, they do not.

20 Every path leads back to the same source: Capital One’s uniform practices, policies, data-sharing

21 ecosystem, and failure to compensate anyone for use of their information. When the same conduct

22 drives every claim and defense and produces a common harm, class certification is not a close call.

23 The Court should grant Plaintiffs’ motion to certify as modified herein.

10 1011, 1022 (9th Cir. 1998)). Assessing predominance “may ‘entail some overlap with the merits of

11 the plaintiff’s underlying claim,’” but “Rule 23 grants courts no license to engage in free-ranging

12 merits inquiries at the certification stage.” Amgen Inc. v. Connecticut Ret. Plans & Tr. Funds, 568

14 the alleged concern about a proposed class is that it exhibits not some ‘fatal dissimilarity but rather,

15 a fatal similarity’ as to an element of plaintiffs’ cause of action, the question [about the proposed

16 class] is properly engaged with on summary judgment, not class certification.” Jimenez v. Menzies

18 Bouaphakeo, 577 U.S. 442, 457 (2016)). No question identified by Plaintiffs requires individualized

 6      1. Jurisdiction and Service

 7          Plaintiffs’ Position: It is Plaintiffs’ position that this Court has subject matter jurisdiction over

 8 this matter pursuant to 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 and 1332(d) and has supplemental jurisdiction over

 9 Plaintiffs’ state-law claims pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1367. No issues exist regarding personal

10 jurisdiction or venue, and all parties have been served. As explained in their opposition to Capital

11 One’s pending motion to dismiss (which, in effect, is really a motion for summary judgment),

12 Plaintiffs have standing to assert the claims they brought. See ECF No. 238.

13          Capital One’s Position: As explained in Capital One’s pending motion to dismiss, this Court

14 lacks subject-matter jurisdiction over Plaintiffs’ claims. See ECF No. 219.

15      2. Facts

16          Plaintiffs’ Position: Capital One operates and encourages its customers to use its website

17 https://www.CapitalOne.com on which customers can apply for credit cards. Plaintiffs are customers

18 of Capital One who used Capital One’s website to seek pre-approval or to apply for credit cards.

19 Capital One secretly collects consumers’ non-public financial and personal information while they

20 are engaged in the pre-approval and application process and sends that information to an ecosystem

21 of concealed third-party trackers from Meta, Google, Adobe, and Skai/Kenshoo to more effectively

22 market its products, generate more sales, and to save millions on the cost of marketing because

23 marketing with the use of non-public financial and personal information is much more effective than

24 general marketing without it. Plaintiffs allege that Capital One accomplishes this through two

25 complementary tracking systems – server-to-server technologies and tracking tags. Plaintiffs allege

26 that the tracking systems on Capital One’s website are used to collect and disclose their non-public

27 personal and financial information to third parties entirely without their knowledge or authorization.

28 Plaintiffs additionally allege that undisclosed fourth parties also had access to that data and that
                                                -1-

 1 anyone using Google or Facebook, for example, to market their products could benefit from Plaintiffs’

 2 private information being shared with Google and Facebook by Capital One. Plaintiffs moved for

 3 Class Certification on January 19, 2026 (see ECF No. 186).

 4          After Plaintiffs circulated a draft Joint Case Management Statement containing the above

 5 single paragraph summarizing their position, Capital One responded by inserting a lengthy statement

 6 of its own—one that merely repackages the same tired mischaracterizations it has repeated across its

 7 filings about the evidence, Plaintiffs’ testifying expert, and Plaintiffs’ theory of the case. These

 8 aspersions are improper in a case management statement. They serve only to inflame, not to assist the

 9 Court.

10          Notwithstanding Capital One’s inappropriate maneuver, discovery showed that Capital One

11 transmitted substantial data to third parties, and those third parties even retained contractual rights to

12 use the data for their own purposes. ECF No. 238 at 4-12. As shown in Plaintiffs’ motion for sanctions

13 and pending motion for de novo review, server-to-server technologies—which merely serve as a

14 complementary counterpoint to the browsing tag technologies—have always been part of this case,

15 which has broadly challenged Capital One’s use of “tracking technologies” on its website. No court

16 has said these two technologies are different—just the opposite, the court in Griffith v. TikTok, Inc.,

17 noted how similar the two technologies are. 2024 WL 5279224, at *2 (C.D. Cal. Dec. 24, 2024). And

18 finally, Capital One’s transmission practices fall outside the scope of what its privacy policy

19 disclosed. Thus, discovery has confirmed Plaintiffs’ position.

20          Capital One’s Position: Fact discovery closed on November 7, 2025, and expert discovery

21 closed on January 9, 2026. See ECF No. 143. Plaintiffs survived a motion to dismiss based on their

22 core allegation that Capital One used “online tracking technologies” that purportedly disclosed to

23 third parties Plaintiffs’ “Personal and Financial Information” entered when submitting a “credit card

24 application.” Compl. ¶¶ 2–4. According to the Complaint, the “only purpose” for these transmissions

25 was “to be used for [] Third Party and fourth parties’ marketing and sales purposes,” which allegedly

26 caused Plaintiffs to experience an “injury-in-fact.” Id. ¶¶ 47, 220. Discovery did not generate any

27 evidence supporting this allegation. To the contrary, in August 2025, Plaintiffs produced the report

28 and supporting materials from the consulting expert report referenced in their Complaint, which
                                                -2-

 5 new theory of the case focused on so-called “server-side” or “server-to-server technologies.” ECF

 6 No. 194-2 ¶¶ 28-30.         Those technologies function very differently from the browser-based

 7 technologies in the Complaint: whereas browser-based technologies allegedly “instantaneously and

 8 surreptitiously” capture information from Capital One’s website, Compl. ¶ 42, server-to-server

 9 technologies send “information directly from the website owner’s server to [the third party’s server]”

10 hours, days, or weeks after information is collected by the website owner. Griffith v. TikTok, Inc.,

11 2024 WL 5279224, at *2, *10 (C.D. Cal. Dec. 24, 2024), appeal filed, No. 25-553 (9th Cir. 2025).

18 sanctions). Moreover, Plaintiffs’ new focus on “server-to-server” technologies did not uncover any

19 transmissions for advertising for either Plaintiff before this suit was filed.

20          Discovery has only confirmed what Capital One has steadfastly maintained throughout this

21 litigation: Capital One implemented robust data governance processes to safeguard consumer

22 privacy, and Capital One does not share any personal information with third parties unless a customer

23 agrees to Capital One’s privacy policy, which explains the types of data Capital One may collect, how

26 same information was transmitted to the same third parties for the same purpose for all class members

27 over the entire class period; in fact, Plaintiffs’ own experiences disprove their contention that Capital

28 One intercepted and transmitted the same information during the class period.
